body.objective: Students will be able to adapt a story for story theatre.
body.iCan: I can adapt a story for story theatre.
successCriteria: I can adapt a story into a story theatre script
I can share narration among performers
I can use bodies and voices to create setting and effects
body.hook: In story theatre, the actors are the scenery, the sound effects and the narrators all at once. A group of performers can become a forest, a storm and a talking fox in seconds. It started in the 1970s and is still used to bring folk tales to life.

vocabulary.definition: A style where actors narrate a story and act it out, often playing objects and settings too.
A person who tells the story to the audience.
Changing a story from one form, such as a book, into another, such as a play.
A traditional story passed down through generations.
Several performers taking turns telling the story.
Sound effects made with voices and bodies to create a setting.

study.title: Stories Come Alive
study.question: How can a group adapt and perform a story using story theatre?
study.passage:
Activities (written for this lesson):
1. Watch and discuss: The teacher models story theatre with three volunteers: "Once upon a time (narrator), a tall tree (one actor becomes the tree) stood beside a river (two actors ripple their arms)."
2. Choose a story (5 minutes): Groups of five choose a short folk tale or fable, for example Aesop's "The Lion and the Mouse," "The Tortoise and the Hare," or a traditional story the group knows and has permission to tell.
3. Adapt (15 minutes): Break the story into 5–7 key moments. For each, write one or two narration lines and decide who plays which character, object or setting. Share narration so everyone speaks. Characters can narrate their own actions: "The hare yawned. 'I have plenty of time.'"
4. Soundscape (10 minutes): Add vocal and body sound effects: wind, footsteps, birds, a crowd.
5. Rehearse (15 minutes): Run the piece twice.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; story theatre was popularized by Paul Sills in the late 1960s and 1970s.
steps: Write shared narration and assign roles
discussion: Which moment was hardest to adapt? Why?
How did shared narration keep everyone involved?
Which object or setting did actors create best?
How did the soundscape change the mood?
study.product: Write a story theatre script of 5–7 moments with shared narration, roles and sound effects for your group.

body.objective: Students will be able to use stage areas in a performance.

successCriteria: I can name the nine stage areas

body.hook: Directors talk in a special code: "Cross downstage left." "Move upstage centre." Without it, rehearsals would be chaos. Learning the stage map lets everyone move to the right spot every time.

vocabulary.definition: The nine sections of the stage used to describe positions.

The actor's right when facing the audience.

study.title: Mapping the Stage
study.question: How do stage areas help performers and directors?
study.passage:
The stage map (written for this lesson): The stage is divided into nine areas, named from the actor's point of view facing the audience:
Back row: upstage right (USR), upstage centre (USC), upstage left (USL).
Middle row: stage right (SR), centre stage (CS), stage left (SL).
Front row: downstage right (DSR), downstage centre (DSC), downstage left (DSL).
Why "upstage"? Old theatres had raked stages that sloped up toward the back, so actors literally walked up.
Activities: 1. Tape a nine-square grid on the floor. 2. Stage area game (10 minutes): the leader calls an area; everyone moves there. Speed up. 3. Strong areas (5 minutes): Discuss which areas feel most powerful (often downstage centre) and why. 4. Apply (25 minutes): Re-block your story theatre piece: decide where each moment happens and why. Write the stage areas into your script.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

Write stage areas into your script
discussion: Why are stage left and right named from the actor's view?
Which area feels most powerful? Why?

study.product: Add stage areas to every moment of your story theatre script and explain where you placed the most important moment and why.

body.objective: Students will be able to perform and give audience feedback.
body.iCan: I can perform and give audience feedback.
successCriteria: I can perform my story theatre piece with focus and commitment
I can show good audience etiquette
I can give specific, helpful feedback on performances
body.hook: A performance isn't complete without an audience. And good audiences do their part: they listen, respond, respect the performers and give feedback that helps. Today you perform and you practise being a great audience.

vocabulary.definition: Respectful behaviour while watching a performance.
Confidence and energy that holds the audience's attention.
One strength and one area to improve.

study.title: Showtime
study.question: How do performers and audiences both make a performance succeed?
study.passage:
Audience etiquette (written for this lesson): Phones away; stay seated and quiet; watch the performers; laugh and react honestly but don't talk; applaud at the end; never call out or mock.
Performer checklist: Hold your neutral position before starting; project and articulate; stay in character even if something goes wrong; hold the final freeze; take a group bow together.
Feedback (written for this lesson): After each piece, two audience members give a glow (a specific strength) and a grow (one specific suggestion), linked to the skills studied: voice, gesture, tableau, stage areas, narration. Strong: "Glow: the river made from four bodies rippling looked amazing. Grow: the narrator at stage left was hard to hear; try projecting to the back wall." Weak: "It was good." "It was boring."
Self-reflection: After performing, each group answers: What went well? What went wrong and how did we handle it? What would we change?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Review audience etiquette and the performer checklist
Watch other groups with good etiquette
discussion: What made your group's performance strong?
How did you handle any mistakes?
Why does audience behaviour affect performers?
study.product: Perform your piece, give glow and grow feedback to two groups, and write a group reflection on what went well and what you'd change.
